doc.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: Latin jazz as a legitimate genre: Dizzy, Chano Pozo, Machito and Bauza
summary: He defends Latin jazz, crediting Machito and Mario Bauza, and Dizzy Gillespie bringing in Chano Pozo in 1945; his own group is a jazz band with congas.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yes. Because that happens with my quintet, a lot of people come to me and say, “You let these guys shine.” I lay out sometimes because I have a Latin jazz quintet but I consider my group jazz-Latin. It’s a jazz band with congas. That’s how I approach. Because once you hear “Latin music,” they think you’ve got a singer, it’s a salsa band, so Latin jazz is a whole genre in itself. One guy on a radio station asked me, “Do you think Latin jazz is a legitimate genre?” I said, “What.” I said okay. Well who’s the founder of that? Who is the guy that made it popular. It’s Dizzy and Chano. In 1945 when Chano Pozo came from Cuba, Mario Bauza introduced him to Dizzy Gillespie. This is where “Manteca,” “Tin Tin Deo” all those numbers — so if you don’t think Dizzy Gillespie is legitimate enough — he’s the one who is the father of Latin jazz but before him it was Machito and Mario Bauza. Dizzy only made it popular, that hey this music is happening. It’s been happening big band style since the 40s already. So when Chano came in he just mixed in with Diz and that’s the marriage with jazz and Latin see? So therefore then I say you think Dizzy is not legitimate? You say well he’s the best. Well he’s the father of this. You know? So this is why I put him in the spot there you know. That’s what it is.
